I think the main reason why people buy open world games is because they provide a good value for money. You can get 100 hours out of them no problem, and to a lot of people that's appealing. Just being able to hop in the game and pluck away at some relatively easy tasks in no particular order can be very relaxing.

However, I actually really like short, linear games as well. The main reason why people generally don't buy those as much is because they tend to cost the same amount of money, while providing a much shorter experience. There is something really satisfying in actually being able to beat a game in a few days and knowing that you got the full experience without missing anything though.

From my perspective it's not really a question of preference as it is a question of what you get for your money. If you can score a linear game that's designed to just give you a few hours of fun on a steam sale for 5 bucks it's a fantastic investment, but buying one full price often feels like a ripoff.

The irony is that short, linear games can be just as expensive, or more expensive to develop than open world games, since in order to leverage the strengths of following a linear path they need to throw lots of unique setpieces and well acted writing at you. I hope that in the future the industry will have better tools to make unique content cheaply, because that will both increase the ability to price shorter games appropriately, and allow open world games to have less cloned content and more stuff to discover.
